nameStory: Wood horsetail gets its name from its preferred woodland habitat and the resemblance of its jointed, hollow stems to a horse's tail. The delicate, lacy branching pattern of this species makes it look particularly feathery and tail-like compared to its relatives.
description: Wood horsetail is an ancient, primitive plant that looks like a delicate green bottle brush or feathery plume. Instead of leaves, it has jointed, hollow stems with whorls of thin branches that create an intricate, lacy appearance. This is considered the most attractive of all the horsetails, growing in graceful clumps that can reach knee-high in favorable conditions.

idTips.label: Branching Pattern
idTips.description: The branches divide again into smaller sub-branches, creating a distinctly feathery, lacy texture that feels soft and delicate to the touch - like running your fingers through fine green lace

idTips.label: Stem Joints
idTips.description: The main stem has distinct joints or nodes that feel like bamboo when you run your finger along them, with small dark bands marking each joint

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms elegant, upright clumps rather than sprawling colonies, with individual stems arching gracefully outward from the center

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: The entire plant feels remarkably soft and flexible, bending easily without breaking - quite different from the rigid, scratchy feel of rough horsetail

idTips.label: Branch Whorls
idTips.description: Thin branches emerge in circular whorls around the stem at each joint, with each whorl creating a distinctive layered, tiered appearance

habitat: Wood horsetail thrives in moist, acidic soils of coniferous and mixed forests throughout New England's mountains and cooler regions. Look for it in shaded spots along woodland streams, in boggy areas, and on forest floors where the soil stays consistently damp. It's often found growing alongside ferns, mosses, and other moisture-loving woodland plants.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge as pale, cone-like fertile stems that produce spores, followed by the distinctive green sterile stems with their lacy branching pattern.
seasonality.summer: The feathery green stems reach their full height and most attractive appearance, creating delicate woodland displays in shaded, moist areas.
seasonality.fall: The soft green stems begin to yellow and die back, though they may persist longer than other horsetail species in protected locations.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions die back completely, leaving only underground rhizomes that will produce next year's growth.

funFact: Horsetails are living fossils that dominated Earth's forests 300 million years ago when some species grew as tall as modern trees - today's wood horsetail is a tiny remnant of those ancient giants that once towered over early dinosaurs!
confusionNotes: Wood horsetail's lacy, twice-branched pattern makes it easy to distinguish from field horsetail, which has simpler, unbranched or once-branched stems. Remember: if it looks delicate and feathery like fine lacework, it's wood horsetail; if it's simpler and more bottle-brush-like, it's likely field horsetail.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called horsetails, these plants aren't related to grasses or typical flowering plants at all - they're more closely related to ferns and reproduce by spores rather than seeds. They represent one of the oldest plant lineages still alive today.
compareHints: Wood horsetail stands out from other New England horsetails by its distinctly twice-divided, lacy branching pattern that creates a soft, feathery appearance. Field horsetail has simpler branching, rough horsetail is unbranched and feels sandpapery, and meadow horsetail has a more rigid appearance with less delicate branching than wood horsetail's gossamer-like texture.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Field horsetail is the most common horsetail in New England and differs from its relatives by having the most delicate, finely divided branches - rough horsetail has thick, unbranched stems, while wood horsetail has branches that branch again, creating a more feathery appearance.

Rough horsetail stands apart from other New England horsetails by being evergreen and completely unbranched - other species like field horsetail have distinctive branching patterns and die back in winter.

Dwarf horsetail stands out from all other New England horsetails simply by being dramatically smaller - while field horsetail might reach 2 feet and rough horsetail can tower at 4 feet, dwarf horsetail maxes out around one foot tall.
Among New England's horsetails, water horsetail is the wetland specialist with simple unbranched stems.
Variegated horsetail is much smaller and more delicate than rough horsetail, lacks the branching side shoots of field horsetail, and stays more compact than water horsetail.
Meadow horsetail stands out from other New England horsetails by its preference for shaded, moist areas and its distinctly delicate, feathery branching pattern.
Marsh horsetail differs from its common relative field horsetail by preferring wetter habitats and having more delicate, less robust branching.
